Galbanum
GAL-buh-num
noun
From Hebrew chelbenāh, a bitter, pungent gum-resin bled from a Persian umbellifer; a KJV hapax, named once only, among the sweet spices of the holy incense (Exo 30:34).

Biblical Definition

Galbanum is one of the four sweet spices the LORD commanded for the perfume of the sanctuary: “Take unto thee sweet spices, stacte, and onycha, and galbanum; these sweet spices with pure frankincense” (Exo 30:34). It is a word that occurs but once in all Scripture, and that is fitting, for galbanum by itself is no sweet thing at all. Left alone its odour is bitter and rank, the sap of a rough desert plant; yet the apothecary was commanded to temper it “together, pure and holy” (Exo 30:35), and in the compound its very sharpness fixes and deepens the fragrance of the whole. The confection was beaten small and set “before the testimony in the tabernacle of the congregation” (Exo 30:36), most holy, and it typifies the prayers of the saints ascending at the golden altar (Rev 8:3). Let the reader mark the mercy in the recipe: the LORD would have a bitter gum in His holy perfume. So He gathers into the communion of saints the sharp and the sorrowful, the afflicted and the plain, and by the tempering of His Spirit their very griefs are made to sweeten the incense of the church. What is bitter alone is precious in the compound, when the great Apothecary mingles it.

Webster 1828 Definition

A bitter gum-resin, one of the four sweet spices of the holy incense, named but once in all Scripture.

expand to see more

GALBANUM, a resinous, strong-scented gum drawn from an eastern umbelliferous plant.

Named once only, among the sweet spices of the sanctuary’s incense (Exo 30:34).

Bitter and pungent alone, yet fixing and deepening the fragrance of the compound.

Tempered by the apothecary together, pure and holy, and beaten very small.

A figure of the sharp and sorrowful gathered into the holy communion of prayer.

Key Scripture

Exo 30:34 — "And the LORD said unto Moses, Take unto thee sweet spices, stacte, and onycha, and galbanum; these sweet spices with pure frankincense: of each shall there be a like weight:"

Exo 30:35 — "And thou shalt make it a perfume, a confection after the art of the apothecary, tempered together, pure and holy:"

Exo 30:36 — "And thou shalt beat some of it very small, and put of it before the testimony in the tabernacle of the congregation, where I will meet with thee: it shall be unto you most holy."

Rev 8:3 — "And another angel came and stood at the altar, having a golden censer; and there was given unto him much incense, that he should offer it with the prayers of all saints upon the golden altar which was before the throne."

Modern Corruption

Not a contested doctrine but a bitter spice, galbanum recovers the truth that the LORD would have the sharp and sorrowful mingled into His holy fragrance.

expand to see more

The temptation galbanum rebukes is the age’s craving for the smooth and the sweetened — the refusal of anything bitter, sharp, or hard in worship and in life. Men would strain out every pungent thing, and so lose the very note that fixes the fragrance; a religion of nothing but honey turns cloying, and a fellowship that will bear no bitter member soon has no depth of savour at all.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the wisdom of the great Apothecary, who mingles bitter with sweet by design. Galbanum alone is rank; tempered pure and holy it perfects the perfume of the sanctuary. So the LORD gathers the afflicted into the communion of prayer, and by His Spirit makes their griefs to sweeten the incense that rises before the testimony.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

From the Hebrew for a bitter gum-resin, galbanum is the once-named sharp spice tempered into the holy incense.

expand to see more

Galbanum — Hebrew chelbenāh, a pungent gum-resin.

A hapax: named once only, in Exodus 30:34.

Bitter alone, it fixes and deepens the compound’s fragrance.

Beaten small and set before the testimony, most holy (Exo 30:36).

A figure of prayer and of the afflicted gathered into the saints’ incense (Rev 8:3).
